items.question: When do you use Task.Run versus async/await?
items.answer: async/await frees threads during I/O — network, disk, database. Task.Run queues CPU-bound work to the thread pool so you do not block the ASP.NET request thread during hashing or parsing. Do not Task.Run an already async method just to be async. Parallel and PLINQ partition CPU work across cores when each item is expensive enough to justify coordination overhead.
followUps: What happens if you Parallel.ForEach inside a request that already uses the thread pool heavily?
How does this differ from Node worker_threads?
items.sixtySeconds: async for I/O wait. Task.Run for CPU on pool. Never confuse them. PLINQ for big CPU-bound LINQ.

items.question: Why must you never lock across an await?
items.answer: lock is thread-scoped mutual exclusion. await releases the thread but does not release lock — other threads block on the lock while the holder is not even running. Under load you serialize the entire service and can deadlock with the thread pool. Release the lock before any I/O. Use SemaphoreSlim for throttling concurrent outbound calls instead of holding Monitor across network waits.
followUps: Can you use lock with Monitor.TryEnter and timeout?
What is the difference between lock and SemaphoreSlim?
items.sixtySeconds: lock plus await equals disaster. Short lock for memory only. Throttle I/O with SemaphoreSlim.

items.question: How do you fix a Redis cache stampede when traffic spikes?
items.answer: Many parallel cache misses on the same key each hit the database. Single-flight: ConcurrentDictionary of in-flight Task per key so one loader runs and others await the same Task. Add SemaphoreSlim to cap total database concurrency across keys. Jitter cache TTL. Never wrap Redis get and database query in one global lock — that serializes all keys.
followUps: How is single-flight like Promise deduplication in TypeScript?
Should cancelled waiters remove the inflight entry?
items.sixtySeconds: Per-key Task coalescing. DB semaphore. No global lock on cache path.

items.question: When would you choose Channel over ConcurrentQueue plus lock?
items.answer: Channel gives async WriteAsync and ReadAllAsync with optional bounded capacity for backpressure. A RabbitMQ receiver can write to a channel and multiple workers read without hand-rolled wait handles. ConcurrentQueue is lower level; you still coordinate completion and blocking. Channels fit producer-consumer pipelines; ConcurrentDictionary fits shared maps.
followUps: How does Channel relate to IAsyncEnumerable?
items.sixtySeconds: Channel for async producer-consumer with backpressure. ConcurrentDictionary for shared maps.
